lesson.title: Same Question, Many Populations
lesson.summary: A test for homogeneity compares the distribution of one categorical variable across two or more independent groups, using a two-way table whose own row and column totals generate the expected counts.
lesson.body:
A goodness-of-fit test compares one sample to an outside claim about a single categorical variable. A test for homogeneity asks a different kind of question: does one categorical variable have the same distribution across two or more separate groups or populations? The word homogeneity literally means sameness, and that is exactly what the null hypothesis claims, that the distribution of some response variable looks the same no matter which group you are looking at.

The key structural feature of a homogeneity setting is that the groups are fixed by the way the data were collected, before you ever look at the response variable. You take separate, independent random samples from each group, then record the same categorical variable in each one. The results naturally organize into a two-way table: one variable's categories running down the rows, and the groups running across the columns, with each cell holding a count.

Here is a full worked example. Suppose independent random samples are taken from three schools: 80 students from School A, 90 from School B, and 70 from School C, and each student is asked whether they prefer to study alone, in a group, or with a tutor. The results:

School A, n equals 80: Alone 30, Group 35, Tutor 15
School B, n equals 90: Alone 25, Group 40, Tutor 25
School C, n equals 70: Alone 20, Group 30, Tutor 20

Row totals: Alone 75, Group 105, Tutor 60. Column totals: School A 80, School B 90, School C 70. Grand total 240, since both 75 plus 105 plus 60, and 80 plus 90 plus 70, equal 240.

Unlike a goodness-of-fit test, homogeneity has no outside claim to generate expected counts from, so the expected count in each cell instead comes straight from the table's own margins, using the two-way table formula: expected count equals row total times column total, divided by grand total. For Alone and School A: 75 times 80, divided by 240, equals 6000 divided by 240, equals 25. Working through every cell the same way gives this expected count table:

School A: Alone 25, Group 35, Tutor 20
School B: Alone 28.125, Group 39.375, Tutor 22.5
School C: Alone 21.875, Group 30.625, Tutor 17.5

Every expected count is at least 5, the smallest is 17.5, so the large counts condition is comfortably satisfied. Now apply the same chi-square recipe from the calculating chi-square chapter, cell by cell:

Alone, School A: 30 minus 25, squared, divided by 25, equals 1.000
Alone, School B: 25 minus 28.125, squared, divided by 28.125, equals 0.347
Alone, School C: 20 minus 21.875, squared, divided by 21.875, equals 0.161
Group, School A: 35 minus 35, squared, divided by 35, equals 0.000
Group, School B: 40 minus 39.375, squared, divided by 39.375, equals 0.010
Group, School C: 30 minus 30.625, squared, divided by 30.625, equals 0.013
Tutor, School A: 15 minus 20, squared, divided by 20, equals 1.250
Tutor, School B: 25 minus 22.5, squared, divided by 22.5, equals 0.278
Tutor, School C: 20 minus 17.5, squared, divided by 17.5, equals 0.357

Summing all nine terms gives X squared is approximately 3.42. The degrees of freedom for a two-way table are rows minus 1 times columns minus 1, here 3 minus 1 times 3 minus 1 equals 4. With 4 degrees of freedom, a chi-square statistic of 3.42 sits close to that distribution's median of about 3.36, giving a large P-value, roughly 0.49 from technology, far above any typical alpha level. That points toward failing to reject the claim that the distribution is the same across schools, a decision this unit's later conclusion chapter will make precise.

Notice that the mechanics here are identical to the goodness-of-fit calculation, subtract, square, divide by expected, sum. Only the source of the expected counts has changed, from an outside claim to the table's own row and column totals.
